notice: RN bank batch 27: Maternity II: labor, birth and fetal monitoring. DRAFT - every question must be reviewed by an RN or nurse educator before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: Which finding best distinguishes true labor from false labor?

rationale.correct: True labor: regular contractions that grow stronger and change the cervix.

perOption.a: Only true labor changes the cervix.
perOption.c: This is typical of false labor.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Distinguish true labor from false labor.

questions.stem: When does the second stage of labor begin and end?

options.text: From full cervical dilation (10 cm) to the birth of the baby
From the start of labor to full dilation
From the birth of the baby to delivery of the placenta

rationale.correct: Stages: 1 (dilation), 2 (birth of the baby), 3 (placenta), 4 (recovery, 1 to 4 hours).

perOption.a: This is the pushing stage.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: The fetus is in a left occiput anterior (LOA) position. Where should the nurse place the Doppler to hear the fetal heart?

options.text: Left lower quadrant of the abdomen

rationale.correct: Fetal heart tones are heard best over the fetal back.

perOption.a: With a head-down fetus with its back toward the left, heart tones are loudest below the umbilicus on the left.
perOption.b: This suits a right-sided breech position.
perOption.c: This suits a left-sided breech position.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Locate fetal heart tones by fetal position.

questions.stem: The fetal monitor shows decelerations that mirror each contraction, starting and ending with it. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Continue to monitor; early decelerations are benign
Prepare for an emergency cesarean birth

rationale.correct: Early decelerations come from head compression; no action is needed.

perOption.a: Early decelerations come from head compression and are reassuring.
perOption.c: This isn't required for early decelerations.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A client receiving oxytocin has repeated late decelerations. What should the nurse do first?

rationale.correct: Late decelerations (placental insufficiency): stop oxytocin, reposition to the side, give an IV bolus, consider oxygen per protocol and notify the provider.

perOption.a: Stopping oxytocin reduces contractions and improves blood flow to the placenta.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: The fetal monitor shows abrupt, V-shaped decelerations with no consistent link to contractions. What should the nurse do first?

rationale.correct: Variable decelerations: reposition, check for cord prolapse and consider amnioinfusion.

perOption.a: Variable decelerations come from cord compression; repositioning may relieve it.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: For each fetal heart rate pattern, indicate its most likely cause.

rationale.correct: VEAL CHOP: Variable–Cord, Early–Head, Accelerations–OK, Late–Placenta.

perOption.r1:c1: Early decelerations mirror contractions from head compression.
perOption.r1:c4: Early decelerations are benign but come from head compression.
perOption.r2:c2: Abrupt V-shaped drops come from cord compression.
perOption.r2:c4: This isn't a sign of well-being.
perOption.r3:c3: Late drops come from reduced blood flow to the placenta.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Match fetal heart rate patterns to their causes.

questions.stem: What is the normal baseline fetal heart rate?

rationale.correct: FHR baseline: 110 to 160 beats/min with moderate variability (6 to 25 beats/min).

perOption.a: This is the normal baseline range.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the normal fetal heart rate.

questions.stem: After the membranes rupture, the nurse sees the umbilical cord at the vaginal opening. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Push the presenting part up off the cord with a gloved hand and call for help
Push the cord back into the vagina

rationale.correct: Cord prolapse: relieve pressure, use knee-chest or Trendelenburg position, give oxygen and prepare for urgent birth.

perOption.a: Relieving pressure on the cord keeps oxygen flowing to the fetus.
perOption.d: The nurse must stay and relieve the compression.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: The client's membranes have just ruptured. What should the nurse assess first?

options.text: The color of the client's urine

rationale.correct: After rupture of membranes: check the FHR first, then the color, amount and odor of the fluid.

perOption.a: Cord prolapse can occur when the membranes rupture.
perOption.c: This is checked, but the FHR comes first.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: The amniotic fluid is green-tinged. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Notify the provider and make sure the newborn resuscitation team is available
Give the client oxygen and nothing else

rationale.correct: Meconium-stained fluid: monitor the FHR closely and prepare for newborn resuscitation.

perOption.a: Meconium-stained fluid may mean fetal stress and risk of aspiration.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A client receiving oxytocin has contractions every 90 seconds, each lasting 100 seconds. What should the nurse do first?

rationale.correct: Tachysystole: more than 5 contractions in 10 minutes; stop oxytocin, reposition, give fluids and notify the provider.

perOption.a: This is tachysystole, which reduces placental blood flow.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: Ten minutes after an epidural is placed, a laboring client's blood pressure falls to 88/50 mm Hg. What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Turn the client onto her side and increase the IV fluids
Lay the client flat on her back

rationale.correct: Epidural hypotension: side-lying position, IV bolus, notify the provider (ephedrine or phenylephrine) and monitor the FHR.

perOption.a: Epidurals cause vasodilation; positioning and fluids restore blood pressure.
perOption.c: This isn't the nurse's first action.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to hypotension after an epidural.

questions.stem: A laboring client with an epidural has a bulge above the pubic bone and the fetal head isn't descending. What should the nurse check?

rationale.correct: Check the bladder often during labor, especially with an epidural.

perOption.a: Epidurals reduce the urge to void; a full bladder can block descent.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A client dilated to 9 cm is irritable, nauseated and says, "I can't do this anymore." Which phase of labor is she in?

rationale.correct: Transition: intense contractions, irritability, nausea and an urge to push.

perOption.a: Transition (8 to 10 cm) is the most intense phase.
perOption.b: The latent phase is 0 to about 5 cm, usually calmer.
perOption.d: That is delivery of the placenta.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify the transition phase of labor.

questions.stem: During birth, the baby's head delivers but then pulls back against the perineum (turtle sign). What should the nurse do?

options.text: Help with the McRoberts maneuver and apply suprapubic pressure as directed
Have the client stop pushing and wait 1 hour

rationale.correct: Shoulder dystocia: McRoberts (thighs flexed toward the abdomen), suprapubic pressure, call for help, no fundal pressure.

perOption.a: These maneuvers help free the shoulder in shoulder dystocia.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: During a trial of labor after cesarean, the client has sudden tearing abdominal pain, contractions stop and the fetal heart rate drops. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Uterine rupture: sudden pain, loss of station, FHR changes; emergency cesarean.

perOption.a: A prior uterine scar raises the risk; this is an obstetric emergency.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: Right after her membranes rupture, a laboring client suddenly becomes short of breath, hypotensive and cyanotic, and is oozing blood. What does the nurse suspect?

rationale.correct: Amniotic fluid embolism: support the airway and circulation, start CPR if needed and prepare for DIC.

perOption.a: This is a sudden collapse with DIC, an obstetric emergency.
perOption.c: This doesn't cause cyanosis and bleeding.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A client in labor has intense back pain from an occiput posterior position. Which comfort measure is most helpful?

options.text: Firm counterpressure on the lower back

rationale.correct: Back labor: counterpressure, hands-and-knees or side-lying positions and a birthing ball.

perOption.a: Counterpressure eases back labor.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: Which finding indicates that the placenta is separating?

options.text: A gush of blood, lengthening of the cord and a firm, rounded uterus

rationale.correct: Placental separation usually occurs within 30 minutes of birth.

perOption.a: These are the signs of separation.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: The nurse is alone with a client whose baby's head is crowning. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Support the perineum with gentle pressure, let the head deliver slowly and check for a cord around the neck
Have the client cross her legs

rationale.correct: Precipitous birth: stay, support the head, check for a nuchal cord, keep the baby warm and dry.

perOption.a: This prevents rapid birth and tearing.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
DRAFT: original question written with AI assistance; an RN or nurse educator must check it before candidates rely on it.

questions.stem: A client in preterm labor is receiving terbutaline. Which finding requires the nurse to hold the dose?

rationale.correct: Terbutaline: tachycardia, hyperglycemia, hypokalemia and pulmonary edema.

perOption.a: Beta-agonists cause tachycardia; hold for a heart rate above about 120.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information

questions.stem: A client in labor is positive for group B streptococcus. What should the nurse anticipate?

options.text: IV penicillin during labor, ideally at least 4 hours before birth

rationale.correct: GBS-positive: intrapartum IV penicillin (or an alternative if allergic).

perOption.a: This prevents GBS infection in the newborn.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)

questions.stem: The nurse reviews the fetal monitoring summary for the past hour. Highlight the findings that require intervention.

cells: Late decelerations with three straight contractions

rationale.correct: Concerning patterns: tachycardia, minimal or absent variability and recurrent late decelerations.

perOption.r3: Fetal tachycardia may signal infection or hypoxia.
perOption.r4: Reduced variability may signal fetal hypoxia or acidosis.
perOption.r5: Recurrent late decelerations indicate placental insufficiency.

references: Maternal-newborn nursing texts (e.g. Perry; Lowdermilk)
